opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to where people were standing and what problems they thought they were solving.

If you look at the robotics community that used reinforcement learning for control, say legged locomotion or in-hand manipulation, their framing was very much "control." The question was: given this specific robot, this specific body, how do I get a policy that makes it walk stably, or flip a cube, or recover from a push? Reinforcement learning was a new and powerful tool for that, a better way to get a controller than hand-designing one with classical methods. But the goal was still a skill, usually one skill, on one platform, in a fairly well-defined setting. Nobody in that line of work woke up thinking, "I'm building intelligence."

Embodied intelligence as a concept carries a different ambition. It's not just "the robot can move well." It's that an agent with a body, through perception, interaction, and feedback with the physical world, can come to understand that world, generalize across tasks, handle open-ended instructions, deal with objects it has never seen. It connects to cognition, to language, to reasoning about the scene. So when you talk about embodied intelligence, you're implicitly talking about generality, the brain and not only the cerebellum, if you like.

The RL control people were mostly doing what I'd call cerebellum-level work: low-level motor skills, balance, dynamics. Extremely hard and extremely valuable, but in their own eyes it was robotics and control engineering, not an intelligence problem. And honestly, before large models came along, there wasn't a credible path from "my quadruped walks on rough terrain" to "my robot understands what you're asking and figures out how to do it in a new home." The pieces were too disconnected.

There's also a community and vocabulary issue. "Embodied AI" originally came more from the computer vision and AI side: embodied navigation, embodied question answering, simulated agents in houses. Those people often weren't touching real robots, and the roboticists weren't touching that language. So you had two groups, one with the word "intelligence" but often no real body, and one with real bodies but thinking of themselves as doing control. Only recently, as foundation models matured and people began seriously trying to give them hands and legs, have these threads come together, and only then did people look back and say, oh, that locomotion and dexterity work is actually part of embodied intelligence too, it's the motor foundation the whole thing has to stand on.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as a new, more powerful way to obtain a controller, while the work remained focused on control skills rather than intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what people were actually trying to solve, and what community they saw themselves belonging to.

For a long time, the people doing reinforcement learning for legged locomotion, or for manipulation, were coming out of the classical robotics tradition. Their problem was control. You have a quadruped, you have a dynamics model, you want it to walk over rough terrain without falling. RL was just a better tool for producing a controller than hand-tuned model predictive control. The question they cared about was "does the robot walk," not "does the robot understand anything." So they didn't need a grand framing like embodied intelligence. They would have said, we do robot learning, or we do learning-based control.

The second reason is that the word intelligence carried a lot of baggage. If you say embodied intelligence, you are implicitly claiming something about perception, about reasoning, about generalizing to new tasks and new environments. The locomotion work, as impressive as it was, was mostly trained for one body and one task family. You trained a policy in simulation, you transferred it, and it worked beautifully, but if you asked it to open a door it had no idea. People in that community were honest about this. They knew the policy was a reflex, a very good reflex, not a mind.

The third thing, and I think this is actually the most important, is that the intelligence part of embodied intelligence came from a different direction entirely. It came from vision and from language. The moment large models could look at a scene and tell you what is in it, and could take an instruction in natural language and turn it into a sequence of steps, suddenly the "brain" existed in a form that could plausibly be put into a body. Before that, there was nothing to embody. So the RL control people were building the body and the cerebellum, and nobody was building the cortex. Once the cortex showed up, the whole field got renamed.

Now, in hindsight, I think the RL control work absolutely was part of embodied intelligence. Low-level control is not a solved problem, and whoever builds the general-purpose robot will need both the reflexes and the reasoning. But at the time, from inside that community, calling yourself embodied intelligence would have felt like overclaiming. And robotics people, culturally, are very allergic to overclaiming, because the robot either stands up or it falls down, and everyone can see which one happened.

r001.rationale: The response says their problem remained control and RL was simply a better tool for producing a controller than hand-tuned MPC, framing it as a change in method rather than in the nature of their work.

astra-6.text:
I think they would recognize that their work fits under embodied intelligence, but that wasn’t the terminology they used. They were working on robot learning or control: how to make a robot walk, grasp an object, or respond to a disturbance. The question was whether reinforcement learning could solve that particular problem.

Embodied intelligence gives those problems a broader framing. It asks how an agent’s intelligence emerges through interaction between its body and its environment, bringing perception, action, and learning together. A researcher training a walking policy might focus on control and take the perception system or task definition as given.

So I wouldn’t say their work wasn’t embodied intelligence. Much of it clearly was. They just approached it through a more specific research question, under a different name.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers focused on specific robot learning or control problems and used different terminology, but it does not explain that adopting reinforcement learning was viewed as a change of method within control rather than a fundamental change in the nature of their work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they often saw their work as solving a control problem. You have a robot, a set of observations and actions, and a reward function, and you train a policy to perform a particular task. The questions are: Does it work? Is it stable? Can it transfer to the real robot? They might call that reinforcement learning for robotics without feeling a need to call it embodied intelligence.

But in a broader sense, it certainly belongs to embodied intelligence. The robot learns through interaction with its environment, and what it can learn depends on its body, its sensors, and its actions. So I wouldn’t say those researchers rejected the idea. Their emphasis—and the terminology of their community—was simply different. The newer framing puts those control problems into a larger question: how does an agent develop intelligence through physical interaction with the world?

r001.rationale: The response describes the work as solving a control problem with a robot, observations, actions, and a reward-trained policy, and says the researchers used the robotics reinforcement-learning label without needing a broader one. This conveys reinforcement learning as part of their control framing rather than a fundamental change in what their work was.
